title: Count the Set Bits
statement:
You get n, a 32-bit unsigned word. It is passed as an ordinary non-negative integer from 0 to 4 294 967 295 (232 − 1), so a value with the top bit set arrives as a number of 231 or more, never as a negative number.

Return how many of its 32 bits are 1.

examples.why: That is 2³¹ + 8: bits 31 and 3. In JavaScript, a loop like while (n) { …; n >>= 1 } never ends here. >> copies the sign bit, so n turns negative and gets stuck at −1. >>> shifts in zeros.
Every bit is set. In JavaScript, n | 0 on this value is −1, which shows how the same 32 bits read as a signed number.

hints: You can look at the lowest bit with n & 1. How do you bring the next bit down into that position?
Shift right and repeat 32 times. In JavaScript, which right shift keeps a value with the top bit set non-negative?
Faster: n & (n − 1) clears the lowest 1 bit. Count how many times you can do that before n reaches 0.

explain.intuition:
The plain way: check the lowest bit with n & 1, shift right, and repeat for all 32 positions. The catch in JavaScript is the shift. Bitwise operators see their operand as a signed 32-bit integer, so a value of 231 or more reads as negative. >> keeps the sign by copying the top bit in from the left, and >>> fills with zeros. For unsigned data always use >>>. Python ints have no fixed width and are never negative here, so >> is fine there.

The neat trick: subtracting 1 from n flips its lowest 1 bit to 0 and every 0 below it to 1. So n & (n − 1) is n with exactly its lowest 1 bit removed. Repeat until n is 0, and the loop runs once per set bit instead of 32 times.
steps: While n is not 0: replace n with n & (n − 1) and add 1 to count.
In TypeScript, write (n & (n − 1)) >>> 0 so the value stays unsigned. Otherwise it may go negative, which still works but is harder to reason about.
pitfalls: Using >> in JavaScript inside a while (n !== 0) loop. For inputs with the top bit set, n becomes −1 and the loop never ends.
Testing n % 2 on a value already turned negative by a bitwise operator: in JavaScript −3 % 2 is −1, not 1.
Assuming n.toString(2) shows 32 digits. It drops leading zeros, which is fine for counting but not for anything position-based.

solutions.title: Read the binary string
solutions.idea: Write n in base 2 and count the '1' characters. Fine for a quick answer; it allocates a string each call.

solutions.title: Check all 32 positions
solutions.idea: Bring each bit down to position 0 with an unsigned shift and test it with & 1.

solutions.title: Clear the lowest set bit
solutions.idea: n & (n − 1) removes exactly one 1 bit. The loop runs once per set bit.

followups: This runs millions of times in a hot loop. How would a 256-entry lookup table for 8-bit chunks help?
